summary.text: Expanding the degree- Chebyshev polynomial yields \(C_{13}(X)-2=(X-2)Q(X)^2\), and \(C_{13}(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(13\theta)\) shows that the six shifted cosine values \(2+2\cos(2\pi k/13)=4\cos^2(\pi k/13)\) are roots of the corresponding shifted sextic. These roots are distinct because cosine is injective on \([0,\pi]\), so monicity and degree give the complete linear factorization; reversing that polynomial produces the claimed denominator factorization.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
D(x)=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\]
We prove that
\[
D(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right).
\]

It is convenient first to prove the corresponding factorization of the reciprocal polynomial. Define
\[
P(t)=t^6-11t^5+45t^4-84t^3+70t^2-21t+1
\]
and introduce the auxiliary polynomial
\[
Q(u)=u^6+u^5-5u^4-4u^3+6u^2+3u-1.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
P(t)=Q(t-2). \tag{1}
\]
Thus it will suffice to identify six distinct roots of \(Q\), shifted by \(2\).

We use the normalized Chebyshev polynomials \(C_n\), characterized by
\[
C_0(u)=2,\qquad C_1(u)=u,\qquad
C_{n+2}(u)=uC_{n+1}(u)-C_n(u).
\]
The elementary cosine addition formula implies
\[
C_n(2\cos\theta)=2\cos(n\theta) \tag{2}
\]
for every real \(\theta\) and every nonnegative integer \(n\). Indeed, the assertion is immediate for \(n=0,1\), and the induction step follows from
\[
2\cos((n+2)\theta)
=(2\cos\theta)(2\cos((n+1)\theta))-2\cos(n\theta).
\]

Repeatedly applying the recurrence for \(C_n\) gives
\[
C_{13}(u)
=u^{13}-13u^{11}+65u^9-156u^7+182u^5-91u^3+13u.
\]
Substitution and multiplication now give the following polynomial identity:
\[
C_{13}(u)-2=(u-2)Q(u)^2. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, this is the explicit identity
\[
\begin{aligned}
&u^{13}-13u^{11}+65u^9-156u^7+182u^5-91u^3+13u-2\\
&\quad=(u-2)
\bigl(u^6+u^5-5u^4-4u^3+6u^2+3u-1\bigr)^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
which follows simply by expanding the right-hand side and collecting like powers of \(u\).

For each integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le 6\), put
\[
\theta_k=\frac{2\pi k}{13},
\qquad
u_k=2\cos\theta_k.
\]
By (2),
\[
C_{13}(\nu_k)
=C_{13}\left(2\cos\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right)
=2\cos(2\pi k)=2.
\]
Consequently, (3) yields
\[
(\nu_k-2)Q(\nu_k)^2=0. \tag{4}
\]
We must exclude the factor \(\nu_k-2\). Since \(1\le k\le6\),
\[
0<\theta_k=\frac{2\pi k}{13}\le \frac{12\pi}{13}<\pi.
\]
On the interval \([0,\pi]\), cosine is strictly decreasing, so
\(\cos\theta_k<\cos0=1\). Hence \(\nu_k=2\cos\theta_k<2\), and in particular \(\nu_k-2\ne0\). Equation (4) therefore implies
\[
Q(\nu_k)=0. \tag{5}
\]

Now set
\[
r_k=4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right).
\]
The double-angle identity \(2\cos^2\alpha=1+\cos(2\alpha)\) gives
\[
r_k
=2+2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right)
=2+\nu_k. \tag{6}
\]
Using (1), (5), and (6), we obtain
\[
P(r_k)=Q(r_k-2)=Q(\nu_k)=0
\qquad (1\le k\le6). \tag{7}
\]
Thus the six numbers \(r_1,\ldots,r_6\) are roots of \(P\).

They are distinct. Indeed, suppose \(r_i=r_j\) for some \(1\le i,j\le6\). By (6),
\[
\cos\left(\frac{2\pi i}{13}\right)
=
\cos\left(\frac{2\pi j}{13}\right).
\]
Both angles lie strictly between \(0\) and \(\pi\), where cosine is injective. Therefore
\[
\frac{2\pi i}{13}=\frac{2\pi j}{13},
\]
and since \(\pi>0\), this implies \(i=j\).

The polynomial \(P\) is monic of degree six. By (7), it has the six distinct roots \(r_1,\ldots,r_6\). The factor theorem therefore shows that
\(\prod_{k=1}^6(t-r_k)\) divides \(P(t)\). Both polynomials are monic of degree six, so they are equal:
\[
P(t)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(t-r_k)
=
\prod_{k=1}^{6}
\left(t-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)\right). \tag{8}
\]

It remains to reverse this polynomial identity. For nonzero \(x\), substitute \(t=x^{-1}\) into (8) and multiply by \(x^6\). This gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^6P(x^{-1})
&=x^6\prod_{k=1}^{6}(x^{-1}-r_k)\\
&=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(1-r_kx).
\end{aligned}
\]
From the explicit definition of \(P\),
\[
x^6P(x^{-1})
=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6
=D(x).
\]
Hence, for every nonzero real \(x\),
\[
D(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}
\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right).
\]
Both sides are polynomials, so this equality on all nonzero real numbers is a polynomial identity (and at \(x=0\) both sides are also visibly \(1\)). Therefore
\[
\boxed{
1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6
=
\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right)
}.
\]
This is exactly the claimed factorization of the denominator of the generating function for A122589.
